data.html:
Dark Matter Superfluidity and Galactic Dynamics

Lasha Berezhiani and Justin Khoury Affiliation: Center for Particle Cosmology, Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA 19104, USA
Abstract

We propose a unified framework that reconciles the stunning success of MOND on galactic scales with the triumph of the Λ\LambdaCDM model on cosmological scales. This is achieved through the physics of superfluidity. Dark matter consists of self-interacting axion-like particles that thermalize and condense to form a superfluid in galaxies, with ∼\simmK critical temperature. The superfluid phonons mediate a MOND acceleration on baryonic matter. Our framework naturally distinguishes between galaxies (where MOND is successful) and galaxy clusters (where MOND is not): dark matter has a higher temperature in clusters, and hence is in a mixture of superfluid and normal phase. The rich and well-studied physics of superfluidity leads to a number of striking observational signatures.

The standard Λ\Lambda Cold Dark Matter (Λ\LambdaCDM) model does very well at fitting large scale observables. On galactic scales, however, a number of challenges have emerged. Disc galaxies display a tight correlation between total baryonic mass and asymptotic velocity, Mb∼vc4M_{\rm b}\sim v_{\rm c}^{4}, known as the Baryonic Tully-Fisher Relation (BTFR) Freeman1999; McGaugh:2000sr. Hydrodynamical simulations can reproduce the BTFR by tuning baryonic feedback processes, but their stochastic nature naturally results in a much larger scatter Vogelsberger:2014dza. Furthermore, the mass BoylanKolchin:2011de; toobigtofail2 and phase-space Pawlowski:2012vz; Pawlowski:2013cae; Ibata:2013rh; Ibata:2014pja distributions of dwarf satellites in the Local Group are puzzling.

A radical alternative is MOdified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) Milgrom:1983ca, which replaces dark matter (DM) with a modification of gravity at low acceleration: a≃aNa\simeq a_{\rm N} (aN≫a0a_{\rm N}\gg a_{0}); a≃aN​a0a\simeq\sqrt{a_{\rm N}a_{0}} (aN≪a0a_{\rm N}\ll a_{0}), with best-fit value a0≃1.2×10−8​cm/s2a_{0}\simeq 1.2\times 10^{-8}~{\rm cm}/{\rm s}^{2}. This empirical force law has been remarkably successful at explaining a wide range of galactic phenomena Famaey:2011kh. In the MOND regime, a test particle orbits an isolated source according to v2/r=GN​Mb​a0/r2v^{2}/r=\sqrt{G_{\rm N}M_{\rm b}a_{0}/r^{2}}. This gives a constant asymptotic velocity, vc2=GN​Mb​a0v_{\rm c}^{2}=\sqrt{G_{\rm N}M_{\rm b}a_{0}}, which in turn implies the BTFR.

The empirical success of MOND, however, is limited to galaxies. The predicted temperature profile in galaxy clusters conflicts with observations Aguirre:2001fj. The Tensor-Vector-Scalar (TeVeS) relativistic extension Bekenstein:2004ne fails to reproduce the CMB and matter spectra Skordis:2005xk; Zuntz:2010jp. The lensing features of merging clusters Clowe:2006eq; Harvey:2015hha are problematic Angus:2006qy. This has motivated various hybrid proposals that include both DM and MOND, e.g., Blanchet:2006yt; Bruneton:2008fk; Li:2009zzh; Ho:2010ca; Khoury:2014tka.

In this Letter, together with a longer companion paper future, we propose a novel framework that unifies the DM and MOND phenomena through the physics of superfluidity. Our central idea is that DM forms a superfluid inside galaxies, with a coherence length of order the size of galaxies. The critical temperature is ∼mK\sim{\rm mK}, which intriguingly is comparable to Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) critical temperatures for cold atom gases. Indeed, in many ways our DM behaves like cold dark atoms.

The superfluid nature of DM dramatically changes its macroscopic behavior in galaxies. Instead of evolving as independent particles, DM is more aptly described as collective excitations. Superfluid phonons, in particular, mediate a MOND-like force between baryons. Since superfluidity only occurs at low enough temperature, our framework naturally distinguishes between galaxies (where MOND is successful) and galaxy clusters (where MOND is not). Due to the larger velocity dispersion in clusters, DM has a higher temperature and hence is in a mixture of superfluid and normal phases tisza; london; landau.

The superfluid interpretation makes the non-analytic nature of the MOND scalar action more palatable. The Unitary Fermi Gas, which has attracted much excitement in cold atom physics UFGreview, is also governed by a non-analytic kinetic term Son:2005rv. Our equation of state P∼ρ3P\sim\rho^{3} suggests that the DM superfluid arises through three-body interactions. It would be fascinating to find precise cold atom systems with the same equation of state, as this would give important insights on the microphysical interactions underlying our superfluid. Tantalizingly, this might allow laboratory simulations of galactic dynamics.

The idea of DM BEC has been studied before Sin:1992bg; Hu:2000ke; Goodman:2000tg; Peebles:2000yy; Boehmer:2007um, with important differences from our work. In BEC DM galactic dynamics are caused by the condensate density profile; in our case phonons play a key role in explaining the BTFR. Moreover, BEC DM has P∼ρ2P\sim\rho^{2} instead of ∼ρ3\sim\rho^{3}. This implies a much lower sound speed, which puts BEC DM in tension with observations slepiangoodman.

DM Condensation: In order for DM particles to condense in galaxies, their de Broglie wavelength λdB∼(m​v)−1\lambda_{\rm dB}\sim(mv)^{-1} must be larger than the interparticle separation ℓ∼(m/ρvir)1/3\ell\sim\left(m/\rho_{\rm vir}\right)^{1/3}. From standard collapse theory, the density at virialization is ρvir≃(1+zvir)3​ 5.4×10−28​g/cm3\rho_{\rm vir}\simeq(1+z_{\rm vir})^{3}\;5.4\times 10^{-28}\;{\rm g}/{\rm cm}^{3}, while the virial velocity is v=113​M121/3​1+zvir​km/sv=113\,M_{12}^{1/3}\sqrt{1+z_{\rm vir}}~{\rm km}/{\rm s}, where M12≡M/1012​M⊙M_{12}\equiv M/10^{12}M_{\odot}. Thus λdB​∼>​ℓ\lambda_{\rm dB}\;\lower 3.22916pt\hbox{$\sim$}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\raise 1.1625pt\hbox{$>$}}\;\ell implies

m∼< 2.3(1+zvir)3/8M12−1/4eV.m\;\lower 3.22916pt\hbox{$\sim$}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\raise 1.1625pt\hbox{$<$}}\;2.3\left(1+z_{\rm vir}\right)^{3/8}\;M_{12}^{-1/4}\;{\rm eV}\,. (1)

The second condition is that DM thermalizes, with temperature set by the virial velocity vv. The interaction rate is Γ∼𝒩​v​ρvir​σm\Gamma\sim{\cal N}v\rho_{\rm vir}\frac{\sigma}{m}, where 𝒩∼ρvirm​(2​π)34​π3​(m​v)3{\cal N}\sim\frac{\rho_{\rm vir}}{m}\frac{(2\pi)^{3}}{\frac{4\pi}{3}(mv)^{3}} is the Bose enhancement factor. The rate should be larger than the inverse dynamical time tdyn∼1GN​ρvirt_{\rm dyn}\sim\frac{1}{\sqrt{G_{\rm N}\rho_{\rm vir}}}, such that the coherence length will span the halo. This translates into a bound on the cross section (with meV≡m/eVm_{\rm eV}\equiv m/{\rm eV}):

σ/m∼>(1+zvir)−7/2meV4M122/3 52cm2/g.\sigma/m\;\lower 3.22916pt\hbox{$\sim$}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\raise 1.1625pt\hbox{$>$}}\;\left(1+z_{\rm vir}\right)^{-7/2}m_{\rm eV}^{4}M_{12}^{2/3}\;52~{\rm cm}^{2}/{\rm g}\,. (2)

Later on, we will adopt m=0.6m=0.6 eV as a fiducial value. For M12=1M_{12}=1 and zvir=2z_{\rm vir}=2, the inequality becomes σ/m​∼>​ 0.1​cm2/g\sigma/m\;\lower 3.22916pt\hbox{$\sim$}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\raise 1.1625pt\hbox{$>$}}\;0.1\;{\rm cm}^{2}/{\rm g}. The lower end is consistent with current constraints MiraldaEscude:2000qt; Gnedin:2000ea; Randall:2007ph on σ/m\sigma/m for self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) Spergel:1999mh, though these constraints must be carefully revisited in the superfluid context.

The critical temperature, obtained by equipartition kB​Tc=13​m​vc2k_{\rm B}T_{\rm c}=\frac{1}{3}mv^{2}_{\rm c}, is in the mK range:

Tc=6.5meV−5/3(1+zvir)2mK.T_{\rm c}=6.5\;m_{\rm eV}^{-5/3}(1+z_{\rm vir})^{2}~{\rm mK}\,. (3)

For 0<T<Tc0<T<T_{\rm c}, the system is a mixture of condensate and normal components. The fraction of condensed particles, 1−(T/Tc)3/21-\left(T/T_{\rm c}\right)^{3/2} landaubook, is shown in Fig. 1 as a function of halo mass assuming zvir=0z_{\rm vir}=0. For m​∼<​eVm\;\lower 3.22916pt\hbox{$\sim$}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\raise 1.1625pt\hbox{$<$}}\;{\rm eV}, galaxies are almost completely condensed while massive clusters have a significant normal component.

Superfluid Phase: The relevant low-energy degrees of freedom of a superfluid are phonons, described by a scalar field θ\theta. In the presence of a gravitational potential Φ\Phi, the non-relativistic effective action is ℒ=P⁡(X){\cal L}=P(X), where X=θ˙−m​Φ−(∇→​θ)2/2​mX=\dot{\theta}-m\Phi-(\vec{\nabla}\theta)^{2}/2m Son:2005rv. We conjecture that DM superfluid phonons are governed by the MOND action Bruneton:2007si

ℒ=23​Λ​(2​m)3/2​X​|X|−α​ΛMPl​θ​ρb,{\cal L}=\tfrac{2}{3}\Lambda(2m)^{3/2}X\sqrt{|X|}-\alpha\tfrac{\Lambda}{M_{\rm Pl}}\theta\rho_{\rm b}\,, (4)

where Λ\Lambda is a mass scale, ρb\rho_{\rm b} is the baryonic matter density, and α\alpha is a dimensionless constant. This action should only be trusted away from X=0X=0, as we will see later. The matter coupling breaks the shift symmetry at the 1/MPl1/M_{\rm Pl} level and is thus technically natural. Remarkably (4) is strikingly reminiscent of the Unitary Fermi Gas, ℒUFG​(X)∼X5/2{\cal L}_{\rm UFG}(X)\sim X^{5/2}, which is also non-analytic Son:2005rv.

The phonon action (4) uniquely fixes the properties of the condensate through standard thermodynamics. At finite chemical potential, θ=μ​t\theta=\mu t, and ignoring Φ\Phi, the pressure is given by the Lagrangian density:

P⁡(μ)=23​Λ​(2​m​μ)3/2.P(\mu)=\tfrac{2}{3}\Lambda(2m\mu)^{3/2}\,. (5)

This is the grand canonical equation of state P=P⁡(μ)P=P(\mu) for the condensate. The number density, n=∂P/∂μn=\partial P/\partial\mu, is

n=Λ​(2​m)3/2​μ1/2.n=\Lambda(2m)^{3/2}\mu^{1/2}\,. (6)

Combining these expressions with ρ=m​n\rho=mn, we obtain

P=ρ312​Λ2​m6.P=\tfrac{\rho^{3}}{12\Lambda^{2}m^{6}}\,. (7)

This is a polytropic equation of state P∼ρ1+1/nP\sim\rho^{1+1/n} with index n=1/2n=1/2. In comparison, BEC DM has P∼ρ2P\sim\rho^{2} Goodman:2000tg.

Including phonons excitations θ=μ​t+ϕ\theta=\mu t+\phi, the quadratic action for ϕ\phi is ℒquad=Λ​(2​m)3/24​μ1/2​(ϕ˙2−2​μm​(∇→​ϕ)2){\cal L}_{\rm quad}=\frac{\Lambda(2m)^{3/2}}{4\mu^{1/2}}\left(\dot{\phi}^{2}-\frac{2\mu}{m}(\vec{\nabla}\phi)^{2}\right). The sound speed can be immediately read off:

cs=2​μ/m.c_{s}=\sqrt{2\mu/m}\,. (8)

Using (7), we compute the static, spherically-symmetric density profile of the DM condensate halo. Introducing dimensionless variables ρ=ρ0​Ξ\rho=\rho_{0}\Xi and r=ρ032​π​GN​Λ2​m6​ξr=\sqrt{\frac{\rho_{0}}{32\pi G_{\rm N}\Lambda^{2}m^{6}}}\,\xi, with ρ0\rho_{0} denoting the central density, hydrostatic equilibrium implies the Lane-Emden equation,

(ξ2​Ξ′)′=−ξ2​Ξ1/2,\left(\xi^{2}\Xi^{\prime}\right)^{\prime}=-\xi^{2}\Xi^{1/2}\,, (9)

with boundary conditions Ξ⁡(0)=1\Xi(0)=1 and Ξ′​(0)=0\Xi^{\prime}(0)=0. The numerical solution is shown in Fig. 2. It vanishes at ξ1≃2.75\xi_{1}\simeq 2.75, which defines the halo size: R=ρ032​π​GN​Λ2​m6​ξ1R=\sqrt{\frac{\rho_{0}}{32\pi G_{\rm N}\Lambda^{2}m^{6}}}\;\xi_{1}. Meanwhile the central density is related to the halo mass as chandrabook ρ0=3​M4​π​R3​ξ1|Ξ′​(ξ1)|\rho_{0}=\frac{3M}{4\pi R^{3}}\frac{\xi_{1}}{|\Xi^{\prime}(\xi_{1})|}, with Ξ′​(ξ1)≃−0.5\Xi^{\prime}(\xi_{1})\simeq-0.5. Combining these results, we can solve for ρ0\rho_{0} and RR:

ρ0\displaystyle\rho_{0} ≃\displaystyle\simeq M122/5​meV18/5​ΛmeV6/5​ 7×10−25​g/cm3;\displaystyle M_{12}^{2/5}m_{\rm eV}^{18/5}\Lambda_{\rm meV}^{6/5}\;7\times 10^{-25}~{\rm g}/{\rm cm}^{3}\,;
R\displaystyle R ≃\displaystyle\simeq M121/5meV−6/5ΛmeV−2/5 36kpc,\displaystyle M_{12}^{1/5}m_{\rm eV}^{-6/5}\Lambda_{\rm meV}^{-2/5}\;36~{\rm kpc}\,, (10)

where ΛmeV≡Λ/meV\Lambda_{\rm meV}\equiv\Lambda/{\rm meV}. Remarkably, with m∼eVm\sim{\rm eV} and Λ∼meV\Lambda\sim{\rm meV} we obtain DM halos of realistic size. Concretely, as fiducial values we will fix

m=0.6​eV;Λ=0.2​meV.m=0.6~{\rm eV}\,;\qquad\Lambda=0.2~{\rm meV}\,. (11)

This implies R∼125R\sim 125 kpc for MDM=1012​M⊙M_{\rm DM}=10^{12}\,M_{\odot}. In general, we expect this superfluid core to be surrounded by a cloud of DM particles in the normal phase, likely described by a Navarro-Frenk-White profile Navarro:1996gj.

Including Baryons: We now derive the phonon profile θ=μ​t+ϕ⁡(r)\theta=\mu t+\phi(r) in galaxies, modeling baryons as a static, spherically-symmetric source. The equation of motion, ∇→⋅(2​m​|X|​∇→​ϕ)=α​ρb​(r)/2​MPl\vec{\nabla}\cdot\left(\sqrt{2m|X|}~\vec{\nabla}\phi\right)=\alpha\rho_{\rm b}(r)/2M_{\rm Pl}, where X=μ−m​Φ​(r)−ϕ′2/2​mX=\mu-m\Phi(r)-\phi^{\prime 2}/2m, can be readily integrated:

2​m​|X|​ϕ′=α​Mb​(r)8​π​MPl​r2≡κ⁡(r).\sqrt{2m|X|}~\phi^{\prime}=\frac{\alpha M_{\rm b}(r)}{8\pi M_{\rm Pl}r^{2}}\equiv\kappa(r)\,. (12)

There are two branches of solutions, depending on the sign of XX. We focus on the MOND branch (with X<0X<0):

ϕ′​(r)=m​(μ^+μ^2+κ2/m2)1/2,\phi^{\prime}(r)=\sqrt{m}\left(\hat{\mu}+\sqrt{\hat{\mu}^{2}+\kappa^{2}/m^{2}}\right)^{1/2}\,, (13)

where μ^≡μ−m​Φ\hat{\mu}\equiv\mu-m\Phi. Indeed, for κ/m≫μ^\kappa/m\gg\hat{\mu} we have

ϕ′​(r)≃κ⁡(r).\phi^{\prime}(r)\simeq\sqrt{\kappa(r)}\,. (14)

In this limit the scalar acceleration on baryonic particle is aϕ​(r)=α​Λ​ϕ′/MPla_{\phi}(r)=\alpha\Lambda\phi^{\prime}/M_{\rm Pl}. Matching to the MOND result aMOND=a0​aNa_{\rm MOND}=\sqrt{a_{0}a_{\rm N}} fixes α\alpha in terms of Λ\Lambda and a0a_{0}:

α3/2​Λ=a0​MPl≃0.8​meV.\alpha^{3/2}\Lambda=\sqrt{a_{0}M_{\rm Pl}}\simeq 0.8~{\rm meV}\,. (15)

For the fiducial value (11) Λ=0.2\Lambda=0.2 meV, we get α≃2.5\alpha\simeq 2.5.

As it stands, the X<0X<0 solution is unstable. It leads to unphysical halos, with growing DM density profiles. The instability can be seen by expanding (4) in φ=ϕ−ϕ¯​(r)\varphi=\phi-\bar{\phi}(r) to obtain ℒ=sign⁡(X¯)​Λ​(2​m)3/24​|X¯|​φ˙2+…{\cal L}={\rm sign}(\bar{X})\frac{\Lambda(2m)^{3/2}}{4\sqrt{|\bar{X}|}}\dot{\varphi}^{2}+\ldots. Clearly the kinetic term is ghostly for X¯<0\bar{X}<0. (The X>0X>0 branch is stable but does not admit a MOND regime future.)

Since DM in actual galactic halos has T≠0T\neq 0, however, we expect (4) to receive finite-temperature corrections in galaxies. At finite sub-critical temperature, the Lagrangian depends on XX and two additional scalars Nicolis:2011cs

B≡det1/2​∂μψI​∂μψJ;Y≡μ^+ϕ˙+v→⋅∇→​ϕ,B\equiv{\rm det}^{1/2}\partial_{\mu}\psi^{I}\partial^{\mu}\psi^{J}\,;~~Y\equiv\hat{\mu}+\dot{\phi}+\vec{v}\cdot\vec{\nabla}\phi\,, (16)

where ψI​(x→,t)\psi^{I}(\vec{x},t), I=1,2,3I=1,2,3, and v→\vec{v} are respectively the Lagrangian coordinates and velocity of the normal fluid. For instance, consider the 2-derivative operator

Δ​ℒ=M2​(T)​Y2≃M2​(μ^+ϕ˙)2,\Delta{\cal L}=M^{2}(T)Y^{2}\simeq M^{2}(\hat{\mu}+\dot{\phi})^{2}\,, (17)

where we have specialized to the rest frame of the normal fluid, v→=0\vec{v}=0. This leaves the static profile (13) unchanged, but modifies the quadratic Lagrangian by M2​φ˙2M^{2}\dot{\varphi}^{2}, restoring stability for sufficiently large MM. Specifically this is the case for M​∼>​eVM\;\lower 3.22916pt\hbox{$\sim$}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\raise 1.1625pt\hbox{$>$}}\;{\rm eV} future, remarkably of the same order as mm! By the same token it corrects the condensate pressure by an amount Δ​P=M2​μ2\Delta P=M^{2}\mu^{2}, which obliterates the unwanted growth in the DM density profile, resulting in localized, finite-mass halos.

Another possibility is the finite-T Lagrangian

P⁡(X,T)=23​Λ​(2​m)3/2​X​|X−β⁡(T)​Y|.P(X,T)=\tfrac{2}{3}\Lambda(2m)^{3/2}X\sqrt{\left|X-\beta(T)Y\right|}\,. (18)

where β>32\beta>\frac{3}{2}, as required for stability future. The DM condensate pressure is P⁡(μ,T)=23​β−1​Λ​(2​m​μ)3/2P(\mu,T)=\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{\beta-1}\Lambda(2m\mu)^{3/2}, which is identical to (5) modulo the redefinition Λ→β−1​Λ\Lambda\rightarrow\sqrt{\beta-1}\Lambda. The halo density profile is therefore identical.

Including baryons, it is easy to show that (12) becomes

ϕ′2+2​m​(23​β−1)​μ^ϕ′2+2​m​(β−1)​μ^​ϕ′=κ⁡(r).\frac{\phi^{\prime 2}+2m\left(\tfrac{2}{3}\beta-1\right)\hat{\mu}}{\sqrt{\phi^{\prime 2}+2m(\beta-1)\hat{\mu}}}~\phi^{\prime}=\kappa(r)\,. (19)

At small distances (ϕ′2≫m​μ^\phi^{\prime 2}\gg m\hat{\mu}), the solution approximates the MOND profile ϕ′≃κ∼1/r\phi^{\prime}\simeq\sqrt{\kappa}\sim 1/r, and this gives the dominant force on a test baryonic particle future. At large distances (ϕ′2≪m​μ^\phi^{\prime 2}\ll m\hat{\mu}), the solution tends to ϕ′∼κ\phi^{\prime}\sim\kappa, but this is subdominant to the gravitational acceleration due to the DM halo. The transition radius r⋆r_{\star} delineating the MOND regime (r≪r⋆r\ll r_{\star}) from the DM-halo regime (r≫r⋆r\gg r_{\star}) occurs when κ∼m​μ^\kappa\sim m\hat{\mu}. Substituting (12) and approximating μ^\hat{\mu} by its central value ρ02/8​Λ2​m5\rho^{2}_{0}/8\Lambda^{2}m^{5}, we find

rt∼M11,b1/10(MbMDM)2/5meV−8/5ΛmeV−8/15 28kpc,r_{\rm t}\sim M_{11,\,{\rm b}}^{1/10}\left(\tfrac{M_{\rm b}}{M_{\rm DM}}\right)^{2/5}m_{\rm eV}^{-8/5}\Lambda_{\rm meV}^{-8/15}\,28\;{\rm kpc}\,, (20)

where M11,b≡Mb/1011​M⊙M_{11,\,{\rm b}}\equiv M_{\rm b}/10^{11}\,M_{\odot}. For a galaxy with M11,b=3M_{11,\,{\rm b}}=3 and cosmic DM-baryon ratio MDM/Mb=ΩDM/Ωb≃6M_{\rm DM}/M_{\rm b}=\Omega_{\rm DM}/\Omega_{\rm b}\simeq 6, the MOND regime extends to r⋆∼70​kpcr_{\star}\sim 70\;{\rm kpc}.

Relativistic Completion: It is well-known that a superfluid is described in the weak-coupling regime as a self-interacting complex scalar field with global U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry. Consider the relativistic field theory

ℒ=−|∂Φ|2−m2​|Φ|2−Λ4​(|∂Φ|2+m2​|Φ|2)33​(Λc2+|Φ|2)6,{\cal L}=-|\partial\Phi|^{2}-m^{2}|\Phi|^{2}-\tfrac{\Lambda^{4}\left(|\partial\Phi|^{2}+m^{2}|\Phi|^{2}\right)^{3}}{3\left(\Lambda_{\rm c}^{2}+|\Phi|^{2}\right)^{6}}\,, (21)

where Λc\Lambda_{\rm c} makes Φ=0\Phi=0 well-defined. Substituting Φ=ρ​ei⁡(θ+m​t)\Phi=\rho e^{i(\theta+mt)} and taking the non-relativistic limit, we obtain

ℒ=−(∇→​ρ)2+2​m​ρ2​X−Λ4​((∇→​ρ)2−2​m​ρ2​X)36​(Λc2+ρ2)6.{\cal L}=-(\vec{\nabla}\rho)^{2}+2m\rho^{2}X-\tfrac{\Lambda^{4}\left((\vec{\nabla}\rho)^{2}-2m\rho^{2}X\right)^{3}}{6\left(\Lambda_{\rm c}^{2}+\rho^{2}\right)^{6}}\,. (22)

To leading order in gradients we ignore (∇→​ρ)2(\vec{\nabla}\rho)^{2} contributions and integrate out ρ\rho. In the limit ρ≫Λc\rho\gg\Lambda_{\rm c} this gives

ρ2≃Λ​2​m​(X2)1/4=Λ​2​m​|X|.\rho^{2}\simeq\Lambda\sqrt{2m}\left(X^{2}\right)^{1/4}=\Lambda\sqrt{2m|X|}\,. (23)

Substituting this back into (22), we recover the MOND action (given by the kinetic part of (4)) for ρ≫Λc\rho\gg\Lambda_{\rm c}.

A finite Λc\Lambda_{\rm c} implies that MOND is restricted to ρ​∼>​Λc\rho\;\lower 3.22916pt\hbox{$\sim$}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\raise 1.1625pt\hbox{$>$}}\;\Lambda_{\rm c}, i.e., aϕ​∼>​Λcα2​Λ​a0a_{\phi}\;\lower 3.22916pt\hbox{$\sim$}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\raise 1.1625pt\hbox{$>$}}\;\frac{\Lambda_{\rm c}}{\alpha^{2}\Lambda}\;a_{0}. Thus the MOND regime does not apply to arbitrarily small accelerations. By choosing Λc\Lambda_{\rm c} a factor of a few smaller than Λ\Lambda, the predicted departure from MOND can occur around the acceleration scale of the Milky Way dwarf spheroidals, which are well-known to pose a challenge for MOND Spergel; Milgrom:1995hz; Angus:2008vs; Hernandez:2009by; McGaugh:2010yr; Lughausen:2014hxa.

Cosmology: Given their mass, our DM particles are axion-like. The simplest genesis scenario is through vacuum displacement, with DM being generated at a time when Hi∼m∼eVH_{i}\sim m\sim{\rm eV}. This corresponds to a photon temperature of ∼\simTeV, i.e. around the weak scale! The DM rapidly reaches thermal equilibrium with itself and becomes superfluid, but is decoupled from ordinary matter.

Naturally DM is much colder cosmologically than in collapsed structures. The ratio TTc=(v​m4/3ρ1/3)2\frac{T}{T_{\rm c}}=\left(\frac{vm^{4/3}}{\rho^{1/3}}\right)^{2}, which is constant cosmologically, can be evaluated at matter-radiation equality using ρeq≃0.4​eV4\rho_{\rm eq}\simeq 0.4~{\rm eV}^{4} and veq=vi​aiaeq≃eVm​MPlv_{\rm eq}=v_{i}\frac{a_{i}}{a_{\rm eq}}\simeq\frac{{\rm eV}}{\sqrt{mM_{\rm Pl}}}. The result is TTc≃10−28\frac{T}{T_{\rm c}}\simeq 10^{-28}, which is much colder than the typical range 10−6−10−210^{-6}-10^{-2} in galaxies. To obtain an acceptable cosmology, we need Λ\Lambda and α\alpha to assume different values cosmologically. We will denote their cosmological values by Λ0\Lambda_{0} and α0\alpha_{0}.

On a cosmological background, the phonon equation of motion that derives from (4) is given by

dd​t​((2​m)3/2​a3​θ˙1/2)=−α0MPl​a3​ρb.\tfrac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}\left((2m)^{3/2}a^{3}\dot{\theta}^{1/2}\right)=-\tfrac{\alpha_{0}}{M_{\rm Pl}}a^{3}\rho_{\rm b}\,. (24)

Since a3​ρb=const.a^{3}\rho_{\rm b}={\rm const.}, this can be integrated straightforwardly. The resulting (non-relativistic) energy density ρ=m​n=m​Λ0​(2​m)3/2​θ˙1/2\rho=mn=m\Lambda_{0}(2m)^{3/2}\dot{\theta}^{1/2} is given by

ρ=−t​α0​Λ0MPl​m​t​ρb+ρdust,\rho=-t\frac{\alpha_{0}\Lambda_{0}}{M_{\rm Pl}}mt\rho_{\rm b}+\rho_{\rm dust}\,, (25)

where ρdust∼a−3\rho_{\rm dust}\sim a^{-3}. In the matter-dominated era, the baryonic contribution ∼ρb​t\sim\rho_{\rm b}t redshifts as 1/a3/21/a^{3/2}. In order for the superfluid to behave as ordinary dust, the second term should dominate over the first all the way to the present time: ρdust​∼>​α0​Λ0MPl​m​t0​ρb\rho_{\rm dust}\;\lower 3.22916pt\hbox{$\sim$}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\raise 1.1625pt\hbox{$>$}}\;\frac{\alpha_{0}\Lambda_{0}}{M_{\rm Pl}}mt_{0}\rho_{\rm b}. Substituting the age of the universe t0=13.9×109​yrst_{0}=13.9\times 10^{9}~{\rm yrs} and assuming a DM-to-baryon ratio of ρdust/ρb=6\rho_{\rm dust}/\rho_{\rm b}=6, we obtain (with m∼eVm\sim{\rm eV})

α0​∼<​ 2.4×10−5​eVΛ0.\alpha_{0}\;\lower 3.22916pt\hbox{$\sim$}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\raise 1.1625pt\hbox{$<$}}\;2.4\times 10^{-5}\;\tfrac{{\rm eV}}{\Lambda_{0}}\,. (26)

Since θ˙≃ρdust28​m5​Λ0∼1a3\dot{\theta}\simeq\frac{\rho_{\rm dust}^{2}}{8m^{5}\Lambda_{0}}\sim\frac{1}{a^{3}}, the phonon velocity increases with redshift and inevitably results in a breakdown of the non-relativistic approximation, θ˙≪m\dot{\theta}\ll m. In other words, the superfluid becomes relativistic at sufficiently high density. This is consistent with the equation of state (7): w=Pρ=ρ212​Λ02​m6w=\frac{P}{\rho}=\frac{\rho^{2}}{12\Lambda^{2}_{0}m^{6}}. Demanding that it be non-relativistic by matter-radiation equality puts a lower bound on Λ0\Lambda_{0}

Λ0​∼>​ 0.1​eV.\Lambda_{0}\;\lower 3.22916pt\hbox{$\sim$}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\raise 1.1625pt\hbox{$>$}}\;0.1\;{\rm eV}\,. (27)

This is roughly four orders of magnitude larger than the fiducial value Λ=0.2\Lambda=0.2 eV assumed in galaxies. This can be achieved, for instance, if Λ\Lambda depends on temperature as Λ⁡(T)=Λ01+κΛ​(T/Tc)1/4\Lambda(T)=\frac{\Lambda_{0}}{1+\kappa_{\Lambda}(T/T_{\rm c})^{1/4}}, with κΛ∼104\kappa_{\Lambda}\sim 10^{4}. Meanwhile, (26) implies α0​∼<​ 10−4\alpha_{0}\;\lower 3.22916pt\hbox{$\sim$}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\raise 1.1625pt\hbox{$<$}}\;10^{-4}, which is roughly four orders of magnitude smaller than the 𝒪⁡(1){\cal O}(1) value obtained in galaxies. This can be achieved, for instance, if α⁡(T)=α0​(1+κα​(T/Tc)1/4)\alpha(T)=\alpha_{0}\left(1+\kappa_{\alpha}(T/T_{\rm c})^{1/4}\right), with κα∼104\kappa_{\alpha}\sim 10^{4}. Note that the scale Λ′∼α​Λ\Lambda^{\prime}\sim\alpha\Lambda appearing in the phonon-baryon coupling in (4) is nearly temperature-independent.

Gravitational Lensing: In TeVeS Bekenstein:2004ne the complete absence of DM requires introducing a time-like vector field AμA_{\mu}, as well as a complicated coupling between ϕ\phi, AμA_{\mu} and baryons in order to reproduce lensing observations. In our case, there is no need to introduce an extra vector, as the normal fluid already provides us with a time-like vector uμu^{\mu}. Moreover, our DM contributes to lensing, so we are free to generalize the TeVeS coupling.

Suppose matter fields couple to the effective metric

g~μ​ν≃gμ​ν−2​α​ΛMPl​ϕ​(γ​gμ​ν+(1+γ)​uμ​uν),\tilde{g}_{\mu\nu}\simeq g_{\mu\nu}-2\alpha\tfrac{\Lambda}{M_{\rm Pl}}\phi(\gamma g_{\mu\nu}+(1+\gamma)u_{\mu}u_{\nu})\,, (28)

with γ=1\gamma=1 corresponding to TeVeS. In the weak-field limit, this gives h00=−1−2​(Φ+α​Λ​ϕ/MPl)h_{00}=-1-2(\Phi+\alpha\Lambda\phi/M_{\rm Pl}), hi​j=δi​j−2​(Φ+γ​α​Λ​ϕ/MPl)​δi​jh_{ij}=\delta_{ij}-2(\Phi+\gamma\alpha\Lambda\phi/M_{\rm Pl})\delta_{ij}, where ∇2Φ=4​π​GN​(ρb+ρDM)\nabla^{2}\Phi=4\pi G_{\rm N}\left(\rho_{\rm b}+\rho_{\rm DM}\right). Hence the lensing signal arises from a combination of the uμ​uνu_{\mu}u_{\nu} disformal coupling and the DM condensate density profile. Determining the allowed range of γ\gamma will require a detailed study, which is beyond the scope of this paper. What is clear is that there should be considerably more freedom than in TeVeS. It may even be the case that γ=−1\gamma=-1 is allowed, such that the coupling to matter would reduce to a simple conformal coupling.

Observational Implications: We conclude with some astrophysical implications of our DM superfluid.

Vortices: When spun faster than a critical velocity, a superfluid develops vortices. The typical angular velocity of halos is well above critical future, giving rise to an array of DM vortices permeating the disc Silverman:2002qx. It will be interesting to see whether these vortices can be detected through substructure lensing, e.g., with ALMA Hezaveh:2012ai.

Galaxy mergers: A key difference with Λ\LambdaCDM is the merger rate of galaxies. Applying Landau’s criterion, we find two possible outcomes. If the infall velocity vinfv_{\rm inf} is less than the phonon sound speed csc_{s} (of order the viral velocity future), then halos will pass through each other with negligible dissipation, resulting in multiple encounters and a longer merger time. If vinf​∼>​csv_{\rm inf}\;\lower 3.22916pt\hbox{$\sim$}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\raise 1.1625pt\hbox{$>$}}\;c_{\rm s}, however, the encounter will excite DM particles out of the condensate, resulting in dynamical friction and rapid merger.

Bullet Cluster: For merging galaxy clusters, the outcome also depends on the relative fraction of superfluid vs normal components in the clusters. For subsonic mergers, the superfluid cores should pass through each other with negligible friction (consistent with the Bullet Cluster), while the normal components should be slowed down by self interactions. Remarkably this picture is consistent with the lensing map of the Abell 520 “train wreck” Mahdavi:2007yp; Jee:2012sr; Clowe:2012am; Jee:2014hja, which show lensing peaks coincident with galaxies (superfluid components), as well as peaks coincident with the X-ray luminosity peaks (normal components).

Dark-bright solitons: Galaxies in the process of merging should exhibit interference patterns (so-called dark-bright solitons) that have been observed in BECs counterflowing at super-critical velocities exptpaper. This can potentially offer an alternative mechanism to generate the spectacular shells seen around elliptical galaxies shells.

Globular clusters: Globular clusters are well-known to contain negligible amount of DM, and as such pose a problem for MOND Ibata:2011ri. In our case the presence of a significant DM component is necessary for MOND. If whatever mechanism responsible for DM removal in Λ\LambdaCDM is also effective here, our model would predict DM-free (and hence MOND-free) globular clusters.
